lead: A petrol engine needs a different air-fuel mixture at idle, cruise, full load and acceleration. A carburettor uses the suction of the incoming air to draw petrol into it and to change the ratio as conditions change. A mixture set for one condition is wrong for the others: too rich wastes fuel, too lean misfires or knocks. Carburettors ran millions of Indian scooters and cars before fuel injection, and the same mixture-demand idea now drives electronic injection.
prereq: You need: the four-stroke SI cycle and the meaning of air-fuel mixture from the engine fundamentals topic.

blocks.text: Air-fuel ratio (A/F) is the mass of air divided by the mass of fuel entering the engine. Petrol's chemically correct (stoichiometric) ratio is about 14.7:1 by mass. The engine does not always want that ratio. At idle it needs about 12:1, because low air speed, poor vaporisation and leftover exhaust gas dilute the charge. At cruise it runs about 15–16:1 for economy. At full load it needs about 12.5:1 for maximum power. During acceleration it needs a short extra squirt of fuel. Rich means A/F below 14.7; lean means above 14.7.

blocks.where: ṁ<sub>air</sub> and ṁ<sub>fuel</sub> are the air and fuel mass flows in kg/s; A/F is by mass and has no unit.

sections.h3: Air filter, throttle and the simple carburettor

blocks.text: Air first passes the air filter, which stops dust that would grind the cylinder walls, rings and valve seats. Cars and two-wheelers use a dry pleated paper element; tractors in dusty fields use an oil-bath filter, where the air turns sharply over an oil pool that holds the dust. A choked filter adds pressure drop, so less air flows and the mixture turns rich and smoky.

The throttle is a butterfly valve after the venturi, worked by the accelerator. It sets how much mixture enters, and so the power: an SI engine is governed by quantity, not by mixture strength as a diesel is.

A simple carburettor has a float chamber, a fuel nozzle with the main jet at its foot, a venturi, the throttle and a choke. The float and needle valve hold the petrol at a fixed level, and the nozzle tip sits a few millimetres above it so that petrol cannot spill when the engine stops. The air speeds up in the venturi and its pressure falls; this depression lifts petrol out of the nozzle into the air stream. A simple carburettor's mixture grows richer as air flow rises, because the air's density at the throat falls while petrol's does not, so practical carburettors add a compensating jet or an air bleed.

sections.h3: Venturi flow: air and fuel equations

blocks.text: Treat the air as incompressible across the small depression Δp. Bernoulli's equation from the inlet to the throat gives the air flow. The fuel sees the same Δp, less the head needed to lift it by z to the nozzle tip.

ṁa = Cda At √(2 ρa Δp) ṁf = Cdf Af √(2 ρf (Δp − ρf g z))
At is the throat area and Af the jet area in m²; Cda, Cdf are discharge coefficients; ρa, ρf are the air and petrol densities in kg/m³; Δp is the depression in Pa; z is the tip height above the float level in m.

If z is neglected, A/F = (C<sub>da</sub>A<sub>t</sub> ÷ C<sub>df</sub>A<sub>f</sub>) √(ρ<sub>a</sub> ÷ ρ<sub>f</sub>): two fixed areas give one mixture strength. So the main jet cannot give the rich idle, lean cruise and rich full load. At idle the venturi depression is too small, so an idle circuit is needed; the main jet is sized lean for cruise, so a power valve adds fuel at full load; on a sudden opening the fuel lags the air, so an accelerator pump adds fuel.

Active when
Action
rows: Fuel through a port below the throttle and a transfer port just above it; mixture screw sets richness
Fuel through the main jet into the venturi; sets cruise mixture
Vacuum piston lets a spring open an extra jet; about 12.5:1

examples.question: An engine takes 0.045 kg/s of air. The carburettor is set for 15:1 by mass. Petrol density is 750 kg/m³. Find the fuel mass flow and the fuel volume flow.
steps: Volume flow = ṁ<sub>fuel</sub> ÷ density = 0.003 ÷ 750 = 4×10⁻⁶ m³/s = 4 cm³/s (1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³).
examples.answer: Fuel mass flow is 0.003 kg/s (3 g/s) and fuel volume flow is 4 cm³/s.

examples.question: A simple carburettor must supply 7.2 kg/h of petrol at A/F = 15. Air is at 1.013 bar and 27 °C; the venturi depression is 0.065 bar. The nozzle tip is 5 mm above the float level. Take C<sub>da</sub> = 0.85, C<sub>df</sub> = 0.70, petrol density 750 kg/m³ and R = 287 J/kg K, and treat the air as incompressible. Find the throat and fuel jet diameters.
steps: Lift head ρ<sub>f</sub>gz = 750 × 9.81 × 0.005 = 36.8 Pa, so the fuel sees 6500 − 36.8 = 6463 Pa; fuel speed √(2 × 6463 ÷ 750) = 4.152 m/s.
examples.answer: Throat diameter about 19.1 mm and fuel jet diameter about 1.08 mm. Neglecting the 5 mm lift gives 1.079 mm, so z matters little here.

traps: The main jet alone does not set the mixture at all loads; the idle circuit, power valve, accelerator pump and choke add fuel where it falls short.
A/F is by mass, not volume. Rich means low A/F (more fuel); lean means high A/F. Students often reverse these.
Venturi depression is the pressure drop at the throat, not the manifold vacuum. At idle the closed throttle makes high manifold vacuum, but the venturi signal is weak.
In the jet formula the fuel sees Δp minus ρ<sub>f</sub>gz, because it must be lifted to the nozzle tip; and 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa must be converted first.
The choke is for cold start only. Left on, it washes oil off the cylinder walls and causes rich misfire.

quiz.q: Define air-fuel ratio and give the chemically correct value for petrol by mass.
quiz.a: A/F = mass of air ÷ mass of fuel. Chemically correct petrol is about 14.7:1 by mass.

quiz.q: Why does an SI engine need a rich mixture at idle?
quiz.a: At idle, air speed is low, fuel vaporisation is poor and residual exhaust gas dilutes the charge. A rich mixture near 12:1 keeps enough vapour to burn steadily.

quiz.q: Name the parts of a simple carburettor and the five circuits of a practical one.
quiz.a: Float chamber with float and needle valve, fuel nozzle with main jet, venturi, throttle and choke. Circuits: idle, main, power (economy), accelerator and choke.

quiz.q: An engine takes 0.030 kg/s of air and 0.002 kg/s of fuel. Find A/F and state whether it is rich or lean compared with 14.7:1.
quiz.a: A/F = 0.030 ÷ 0.002 = 15. This is slightly lean because 15 is above 14.7.

quiz.q: Why is the nozzle tip set above the float level, and why does a choked air filter make the mixture rich?
quiz.a: With the tip above the level, petrol cannot run out when the engine stops or tilts. A choked filter adds pressure drop, so less air flows for the same fuel and the mixture turns rich.

quiz.q: Explain why one fixed main jet cannot cover idle to full load.
quiz.a: At idle, air flow and venturi depression are too small to draw fuel through the main jet, so an idle circuit is needed. At high load the main jet alone is too lean for power, so a power valve adds fuel. Sudden throttle opening needs an accelerator pump because fuel lags the air. A single jet cannot provide all these changes.

quiz.q: Distinguish the power/economy valve from the accelerator pump.
quiz.a: The power valve responds to low manifold vacuum at high load and opens an extra fuel jet for steady enrichment. The accelerator pump responds to rapid throttle movement and squirts a short extra dose of fuel to cover the transient lag.

beyond: Not for the exam. Carburettors survive in small engines and vintage vehicles, while most new small engines use throttle-body injection that follows the same mixture target. Constant-depression carburettors move a piston to keep the throat depression nearly fixed. Search next for 'constant depression carburettor', 'venturi fuel metering' and 'air-fuel ratio target map'.
